\section{Introduction}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
Recent approaches based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have closed this gap: \citet{autore2024} fine-tune LLMs with structured decomposition for end-to-end extraction, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy.
Yet every one of them outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without any indication of \emph{which sentences} in the document support each prediction.
In deployment contexts where predictions feed into clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, or financial compliance systems, end users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.

The absence of verifiable evidence creates a practical bottleneck.
Relation extraction outputs feed downstream knowledge graph construction and human decision workflows; when a system predicts that a drug interacts with a gene, or that a contract clause implies a liability, practitioners must trace each prediction back to source text before acting on it.
Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
Both produce evidence annotations and improve extraction quality, but encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in extraction accuracy.
The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.

This gap reflects a deeper structural difference in how evidence functions across architectures and scales.
In encoder-based methods such as SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision; the evidence signal regularizes the encoder and improves extraction at minimal cost.
In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
Yet the role of this generation cost is not fixed.
It depends on at least three factors: \emph{model capacity}, where small models appear to benefit from implicit regularization while mid-scale and larger models show approximately neutral impact as capacity absorbs the generation overhead; \emph{optimization paradigm}, where gradient-based methods create destructive trade-offs between evidence and extraction objectives while discrete sample selection avoids them entirely; and \emph{training data quality}, where filtering based on Natural Language Inference (NLI) scores can transform evidence from an optimization burden into a learning scaffold.
Understanding this landscape is a prerequisite for deploying evidence-grounded extraction systems that are both accurate and verifiable.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training paradigms: online reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}), offline preference optimization via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; \citealt{rafailov2023direct}), and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star}).
Our experiments span three model scales with full RSFT evaluation (1.7B, 4B, 8B), 14B validation, two model families, and two datasets across 85+ configurations. They reveal that the role of evidence generation is governed by three interacting factors.
Along the \emph{capacity dimension}, we observe a within-family capacity threshold (within the Qwen3 family): the evidence tax suggests implicit regularization at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp Ign-F1) but is approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B, +0.04pp at 8B).
Along the \emph{paradigm dimension}, we observe a decoupling spectrum in which the strength of optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none); catastrophic extraction collapse co-occurs with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA; \citealt{hu2022lora}) in GRPO, though full-precision GRPO maintains extraction above the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baseline with only mild decoupling (EDCR 0.6318 vs.\ SFT 0.6797), which indicates that the collapse is not inherent to online RL when sufficient precision is available.
Along the \emph{data quality dimension}, RSFT with NLI-based scoring navigates this landscape by selecting high-quality training samples through output filtering rather than applying gradient-based pressure; it improves mean Ign-F1 across tested scales (+1.2 to +6.6pp) while compressing Qwen3 training variance 7.5--17$\times$ and LLaMA variance 4.6$\times$.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We map the \textbf{evidence generation landscape} through a comprehensive empirical study spanning 85+ experiments across three fully evaluated model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B validation, two model families, two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), and three optimization paradigms. We observe a \textbf{scale-dependent evidence tax} with a within-family capacity threshold (Qwen3): beneficial at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp) but approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp). This challenges the assumption that evidence generation uniformly harms extraction.

    \item We characterize a \textbf{decoupling spectrum} that explains why gradient-based paradigms fail at joint evidence-and-extraction generation: RL optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none). We introduce the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR) as a diagnostic metric, validated through per-relation analysis ($\rho = -0.79$, $n = 76$, $p < 0.001$).

    \item We establish \textbf{RSFT with NLI-based scoring} as an effective navigation strategy for this landscape. RSFT improves mean Ign-F1 across tested scales (+1.2 to +6.6pp) with 7.5--17$\times$ Qwen3 variance compression and 4.6$\times$ on LLaMA (complete pairwise seed separation, Cohen's $d{=}2.58$). Our 1.7B RSFT model (51.19 Ign-F1, std 0.09pp) approaches 8B SFT performance (50.19, std 3.23pp) while being 4.7$\times$ smaller and substantially more predictable, enabling deployment-efficient evidence-grounded extraction.
\end{enumerate}

编码器方法已经部分解决了这个需求——有些工作引入了句子级证据监督，还有的通过动态证据检索改进了提取质量——但这些方法仍有局限。

Yet every one of them outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without any indication of \emph{which sentences} in the document support each prediction.
In deployment contexts where predictions feed into clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, or financial compliance systems, end users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.

The absence of verifiable evidence creates a practical bottleneck.
Relation extraction outputs feed downstream knowledge graph construction and human decision workflows; when a system predicts that a drug interacts with a gene, or that a contract clause implies a liability, practitioners must trace each prediction back to source text before acting on it.
Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
Both produce evidence annotations and improve extraction quality, but encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in extraction accuracy.
The community therefore faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while the evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.

This gap reflects a deeper structural difference in how evidence functions across architectures and scales.
In encoder-based methods such as SAIS and DREEAM, evidence retrieval is a binary classification task (does sentence $s_i$ support relation $r$?) that serves as auxiliary supervision; the evidence signal regularizes the encoder and improves extraction at minimal cost.
In LLM-based DocRE, evidence-grounded extraction requires the model to \emph{generate} complete evidence sentences as part of its output sequence, substantially increasing output length and decoding complexity.
Yet the role of this generation cost is not fixed.
It depends on at least three factors: \emph{model capacity}, where small models appear to benefit from implicit regularization while mid-scale and larger models show approximately neutral impact as capacity absorbs the generation overhead; \emph{optimization paradigm}, where gradient-based methods create destructive trade-offs between evidence and extraction objectives while discrete sample selection avoids them entirely; and \emph{training data quality}, where filtering based on Natural Language Inference (NLI) scores can transform evidence from an optimization burden into a learning scaffold.
Understanding this landscape is a prerequisite for deploying evidence-grounded extraction systems that are both accurate and verifiable.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training paradigms: online reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; \citealt{shao2024deepseekmath}), offline preference optimization via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO; \citealt{rafailov2023direct}), and offline reinforcement learning via Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT, building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star}).

Along the \emph{paradigm dimension}, we observe a decoupling spectrum in which the strength of optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none); catastrophic extraction collapse co-occurs with Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA; \citealt{hu2022lora}) in GRPO, though full-precision GRPO maintains extraction above the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baseline with only mild decoupling (EDCR 0.6318 vs.\ SFT 0.6797), which indicates that the collapse is not inherent to online RL when sufficient precision is available.

    \item We map the \textbf{evidence generation landscape} through a comprehensive empirical study spanning 85+ experiments across three fully evaluated model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B validation, two model families, two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), and three optimization paradigms. This challenges the assumption that evidence generation uniformly harms extraction.

\section{Introduction}

Document-level relation extraction (DocRE) requires identifying semantic relations between entity pairs across multiple sentences, a task where encoder-based methods such as \citet{zhou2021atlop} long dominated.
Recent LLM-based approaches have closed this gap: \citet{autore2024} fine-tune LLMs with structured decomposition, \citet{xu2024lmrc} frame it as multi-choice reading comprehension, and \citet{chen2025docksrag} combine retrieval-augmented generation with structured knowledge.
These methods approach or surpass encoder baselines on DocRED \citep{yao2019docred} and Re-DocRED \citep{tan2022redocred} in extraction accuracy, yet every one outputs bare relation triplets $(e_h, r, e_t)$ without indicating \emph{which sentences} support each prediction.
In deployment contexts---clinical knowledge bases, legal due-diligence pipelines, financial compliance systems---users cannot verify a prediction without manually locating its textual basis across a multi-page document.

Encoder-based methods have partially addressed this need: \citet{xiao2022sais} introduce sentence-level evidence supervision as an auxiliary signal, and \citet{ma2023dreeam} extend this with dynamic evidence retrieval through memory attention.
Both produce evidence and improve extraction, but encoder methods now trail LLM-based approaches in accuracy.
The community faces a gap: the most accurate extractors provide no evidence, while evidence-capable methods are no longer competitive.

This gap reflects a structural difference.
In encoder methods, evidence retrieval is classification that regularizes the encoder at negligible cost; in LLM-based DocRE, evidence requires the model to \emph{generate} additional output tokens per triple, increasing output length and decoding complexity.
The na\"{i}ve expectation is that this generation cost always harms extraction accuracy.
Our experiments show this expectation is wrong.
The evidence tax is not a fixed penalty but a landscape shaped by model capacity, optimization paradigm, and training data quality.
Within the Qwen3 family, evidence generation \emph{benefits} extraction at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp Ign-F1, partly through halving output duplication) but is approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B).
Gradient-based optimization amplifies this competition---GRPO collapses extraction under constrained precision, DPO progressively trades extraction for evidence---while discrete sample selection (RSFT) avoids the trade-off entirely by filtering outputs rather than pushing gradients.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and compare three post-training paradigms---GRPO \citep{shao2024deepseekmath}, DPO \citep{rafailov2023direct}, and RSFT (building on STaR; \citealt{zelikman2022star})---across three fully evaluated scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B validation, two model families, and two datasets. Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Evidence generation is not uniformly harmful.} We observe a scale-dependent evidence tax with a within-family capacity threshold: beneficial at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp) but approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B), challenging the assumption that evidence always costs extraction accuracy.

    \item \textbf{Gradient pressure causes evidence-extraction decoupling.} We characterize a decoupling spectrum (GRPO catastrophic $\rightarrow$ DPO gradual $\rightarrow$ RSFT none) and introduce the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio (EDCR) as a diagnostic, validated at per-relation level ($\rho{=}{-}0.79$, $n{=}76$, $p{<}0.001$).

    \item \textbf{RSFT compresses training variance 7.5--31$\times$.} NLI-based sample selection improves mean Ign-F1 across tested scales (+1.2 to +6.6pp); our 1.7B RSFT model (51.19 Ign-F1, std 0.09pp) approaches 8B SFT performance (50.19, std 3.23pp) at 4.7$\times$ fewer parameters, enabling deployment-efficient evidence-grounded extraction.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Limitations}

All results use the DocRED development set; test set submission is pending. Exact-match F1 penalizes surface-form-different entity mentions~\citep{wan2024genres}, likely underestimating absolute extraction capability of generative models, though relative comparisons between methods remain valid.

We evaluate on two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), both derived from Wikipedia. Cross-domain evaluation is constrained by the absence of evidence-annotated DocRE datasets beyond Wikipedia; this limitation is shared by all prior evidence-aware DocRE work (SAIS, DREEAM, EIDER).

We evaluate one algorithm per RL family (GRPO, DPO) with single hyperparameter settings (KL coefficient 0.01, $\beta$ 0.1); other algorithms or settings may produce different decoupling behaviors. CED scoring depends on an external NLI model, and the RSFT ablation uses limited seeds (four for CED, two for flat-NLI). Evidence tax patterns span two model families (Qwen3, LLaMA) but may not generalize to other architectures or scales beyond 14B.

EDCR correlates with extraction quality at both method level ($\rho{=}{-}0.89$, $n{=}7$) and per-relation level ($\rho{=}{-}0.79$, $n{=}76$), but has not been validated against human judgments of evidence-extraction alignment. Future work should assess whether EDCR rankings correspond to practitioner assessments of output quality.

RSFT improves extraction across scales but evidence quality is unchanged (Evi-F1 $\Delta < 0.4$pp at all scales; Appendix~\ref{sec:error_analysis}). CED-based selection filters for joint quality but does not specifically optimize evidence grounding, suggesting that targeted evidence rewards may be needed to improve evidence quality beyond what data selection achieves.

At 1.7B scale, 44.4\% of outputs exhibit repetitive patterns (vs.\ negligible at 4B+); small models may require decoding-time interventions (e.g., repetition penalty) for reliable deployment.

\section{Ethics Statement}

This work uses publicly available benchmarks (DocRED, Re-DocRED) derived from Wikipedia, containing no private or sensitive information. All models are trained on existing annotated data without human subjects involvement. Our evidence-grounding approach aims to improve the verifiability of relation extraction outputs, which supports responsible deployment in high-stakes domains such as clinical and legal information systems by enabling human verification of model predictions. We release code and model outputs to support reproducibility.

lines: We conduct experiments on DocRED~\citep{yao2019docred}, a large-scale document-level relation extraction benchmark containing 3,053 training and 998 development documents spanning 96 relation types. Each document requires identifying relational triples across multiple sentences and grounding each triple with supporting evidence sentences. We use Re-DocRED~\citep{tan2022redocred} for cross-dataset generalization evaluation.
\paragraph{Models.}
-Our primary model is Qwen3-4B. To study scale effects, we additionally train Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B under identical configurations. We include LLaMA-3.1-8B as a cross-family validation point.
+Our primary model is Qwen3-4B. To study scale effects, we also train Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B under identical configurations. We include LLaMA-3.1-8B as a cross-family validation point.
\paragraph{Training.}

All models use LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora} with rank $r{=}64$ and $\alpha{=}128$ over a structured output format that jointly produces relation triples and evidence sentences. For RSFT, we sample $N{=}8$ candidate outputs per document and select the top-$k{=}1$ response ranked by CED scoring (\S\ref{sec:ced}), which combines NLI-based evidence faithfulness with extraction accuracy. GRPO experiments use group sizes $G{=}4$ (QLoRA, 4-bit) and $G{=}8$ (bf16 full-precision LoRA). DPO constructs preference pairs from CED-ranked outputs.

\begin{abstract}

Large Language Model (LLM) based Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) now matches or exceeds encoder baselines in extraction accuracy, yet these methods output bare relation triplets without identifying which sentences support each prediction.
Deployment contexts such as clinical knowledge bases and legal due-diligence systems require verifiable evidence that users can trace to source text.
Encoder-based evidence methods (SAIS, DREEAM) provide supporting sentences but trail LLM approaches in accuracy, leaving a gap between extraction performance and output verifiability.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and compare Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT) across three fully evaluated scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B validation, two model families, and two datasets.
The prevailing assumption is that evidence generation always costs extraction accuracy. Our experiments reveal that this cost is not fixed but forms a landscape shaped by capacity, paradigm, and data quality. Within the Qwen3 family (on the development set), evidence is beneficial at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp Ign-F1) but approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B; positive $=$ cost). Gradient-based optimization amplifies evidence-extraction competition (GRPO catastrophic, DPO gradual), while RSFT with Natural Language Inference (NLI) based scoring avoids decoupling entirely through output filtering rather than gradient pressure.

RSFT compresses training seed variance 7.5--31$\times$ on Qwen3 and 4.6$\times$ on LLaMA (complete pairwise seed separation, Cohen's $d{=}2.58$). Our 1.7B RSFT model (51.19 Ign-F1, std 0.09pp) approaches 8B Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) performance (50.19, std 3.23pp) at 4.7$\times$ fewer parameters. Test-set evaluation preserves model ranking across all evaluated scales (Spearman $\rho{=}1.0$).

\end{abstract}

Encoder-based evidence methods (SAIS, DREEAM) provide supporting sentences but trail LLM approaches in accuracy, leaving a gap between extraction performance and output verifiability.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and compare Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT) across three fully evaluated scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B validation, two model families, and two datasets.
The prevailing assumption is that evidence generation always costs extraction accuracy. Our experiments reveal that this cost is not fixed but forms a landscape shaped by capacity, paradigm, and data quality. Within the Qwen3 family (on the development set), evidence is beneficial at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp Ign-F1) but approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B; positive $=$ cost). Gradient-based optimization amplifies evidence-extraction competition (GRPO catastrophic, DPO gradual), while RSFT with Natural Language Inference (NLI) based scoring avoids decoupling entirely through output filtering rather than gradient pressure.

RSFT compresses training seed variance 7.5--31$\times$ on Qwen3 and 4.6$\times$ on LLaMA (complete pairwise seed separation, Cohen's $d{=}2.58$). Our 1.7B RSFT model (51.19 Ign-F1, std 0.09pp) approaches 8B Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) performance (50.19, std 3.23pp) at 4.7$\times$ fewer parameters. Test-set evaluation preserves model ranking across all evaluated scales (Spearman $\rho{=}1.0$).

\end{abstract}

1	\section{Limitations}
2	
3	Primary development is on the DocRED development set; Re-DocRED test-set evaluation preserves model ranking (Spearman $\rho{=}1.0$) but shows a 18.9--21.9pp absolute drop attributable to higher annotation density (2.82$\times$ more gold triples per document). Exact-match F1 penalizes surface-form-different entity mentions~\citep{wan2024genres}, likely underestimating absolute extraction capability of generative models, though relative comparisons between methods remain valid.
4	
5	We evaluate on two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), both derived from Wikipedia. Cross-domain evaluation is constrained by the absence of evidence-annotated DocRE datasets beyond Wikipedia; this limitation is shared by all prior evidence-aware DocRE work (SAIS, DREEAM, EIDER).
6	
7	We evaluate one algorithm per RL family (GRPO, DPO) with single hyperparameter settings (KL coefficient 0.01, $\beta$ 0.1); other algorithms or settings may produce different decoupling behaviors. CED scoring depends on an external NLI model, and the RSFT ablation uses limited seeds (four for CED, two for flat-NLI). Evidence tax patterns span two model families (Qwen3, LLaMA) but may not generalize to other architectures or scales beyond 14B.
8	
9	EDCR correlates with extraction quality at both method level ($\rho{=}{-}0.89$, $n{=}7$) and per-relation level ($\rho{=}{-}0.79$, $n{=}76$), but has not been validated against human judgments of evidence-extraction alignment. Future work should assess whether EDCR rankings correspond to practitioner assessments of output quality.
10	
11	RSFT improves extraction across scales but evidence quality is unchanged (Evi-F1 $\Delta < 0.4$pp at all scales; Appendix~\ref{sec:error_analysis}). CED-based selection filters for joint quality but does not specifically optimize evidence grounding, suggesting that targeted evidence rewards may be needed to improve evidence quality beyond what data selection achieves.
12	
13	At 1.7B scale, 44.4\% of outputs exhibit repetitive patterns (vs.\ negligible at 4B+); small models may require decoding-time interventions (e.g., repetition penalty) for reliable deployment.
14	
15	\section{Ethics Statement}
16	
17	This work uses publicly available benchmarks (DocRED, Re-DocRED) derived from Wikipedia, containing no private or sensitive information. All models are trained on existing annotated data without human subjects involvement. Our evidence-grounding approach aims to improve the verifiability of relation extraction outputs, which supports responsible deployment in high-stakes domains such as clinical and legal information systems by enabling human verification of model predictions. We release code and model outputs to support reproducibility.
18	
19	% Responsible NLP Research Checklist: submitted via OpenReview form per ARR/EMNLP 2026 guidelines.
20

\section{Limitations}

Primary development is on the DocRED development set; Re-DocRED test-set evaluation preserves model ranking (Spearman $\rho{=}1.0$) but shows a 18.9--21.9pp absolute drop attributable to higher annotation density (2.82$\times$ more gold triples per document). Exact-match F1 penalizes surface-form-different entity mentions~\citep{wan2024genres}, likely underestimating absolute extraction capability of generative models, though relative comparisons between methods remain valid.

We evaluate on two datasets (DocRED, Re-DocRED), both derived from Wikipedia. Cross-domain evaluation is constrained by the absence of evidence-annotated DocRE datasets beyond Wikipedia; this limitation is shared by all prior evidence-aware DocRE work (SAIS, DREEAM, EIDER).

We evaluate one algorithm per RL family (GRPO, DPO) with single hyperparameter settings (KL coefficient 0.01, $\beta$ 0.1); other algorithms or settings may produce different decoupling behaviors. CED scoring depends on an external NLI model, and the RSFT ablation uses limited seeds (four for CED, two for flat-NLI). Evidence tax patterns span two model families (Qwen3, LLaMA) but may not generalize to other architectures or scales beyond 14B.

EDCR correlates with extraction quality at both method level ($\rho{=}{-}0.89$, $n{=}7$) and per-relation level ($\rho{=}{-}0.79$, $n{=}76$), but has not been validated against human judgments of evidence-extraction alignment. Future work should assess whether EDCR rankings correspond to practitioner assessments of output quality.

RSFT improves extraction across scales but evidence quality is unchanged (Evi-F1 $\Delta < 0.4$pp at all scales; Appendix~\ref{sec:error_analysis}). CED-based selection filters for joint quality but does not specifically optimize evidence grounding, suggesting that targeted evidence rewards may be needed to improve evidence quality beyond what data selection achieves.

At 1.7B scale, 44.4\% of outputs exhibit repetitive patterns (vs.\ negligible at 4B+); small models may require decoding-time interventions (e.g., repetition penalty) for reliable deployment.

\section{Ethics Statement}

This work uses publicly available benchmarks (DocRED, Re-DocRED) derived from Wikipedia, containing no private or sensitive information. All models are trained on existing annotated data without human subjects involvement. Our evidence-grounding approach aims to improve the verifiability of relation extraction outputs, which supports responsible deployment in high-stakes domains such as clinical and legal information systems by enabling human verification of model predictions. We release code and model outputs to support reproducibility.

\begin{abstract}

Large Language Model (LLM) based Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) now matches or exceeds encoder baselines in extraction accuracy, yet these methods output bare relation triplets without identifying which sentences support each prediction.
Deployment contexts such as clinical knowledge bases and legal due-diligence systems require verifiable evidence that users can trace to source text.
Encoder-based evidence methods (SAIS, DREEAM) provide supporting sentences but trail LLM approaches in accuracy, leaving a gap between extraction performance and output verifiability.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and compare Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT) across three fully evaluated scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B validation, two model families, and two datasets.
The na\"{i}ve expectation is that evidence generation always costs extraction accuracy. Our experiments reveal that this cost is not fixed but forms a landscape shaped by capacity, paradigm, and data quality. Within the Qwen3 family (on the development set), evidence is beneficial at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp Ign-F1) but approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B; positive $=$ cost). Gradient-based optimization amplifies evidence-extraction competition (GRPO catastrophic, DPO gradual), while RSFT with Natural Language Inference (NLI) based scoring avoids decoupling entirely through output filtering rather than gradient pressure.

RSFT compresses training seed variance 7.5--31$\times$ on Qwen3 and 4.6$\times$ on LLaMA (complete pairwise seed separation, Cohen's $d{=}2.58$). Our 1.7B RSFT model (51.19 Ign-F1, std 0.09pp) approaches 8B Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) performance (50.19, std 3.23pp) at 4.7$\times$ fewer parameters. Test-set evaluation preserves model ranking across all evaluated scales (Spearman $\rho{=}1.0$).

\end{abstract}

165	\section{Why RSFT Avoids Decoupling}
166	\label{sec:rsft_theory}
167	
168	The structural difference between selection and optimization explains why RSFT does not exhibit the decoupling observed in gradient-based methods. GRPO and DPO update model parameters through gradients that optimize a reward signal. When two sub-tasks (extraction and evidence) compete for gradient capacity, the optimizer can discover and exploit the trade-off between them, improving one at the expense of the other. RSFT operates differently: it selects complete outputs and trains on them with standard supervised loss. Because the selection is discrete (accept or reject a full response), there is no gradient pathway through which the model can learn to sacrifice extraction for evidence quality. Only outputs where both extraction and evidence are jointly strong survive the CED filter. This property is not specific to RSFT's design but is a structural consequence of discrete selection over complete outputs: any selection-based method that filters on a joint quality criterion will inherit the same coupling guarantee. The implication for practitioners is direct: when optimizing for multiple coupled generation objectives, selection-based methods preserve inter-objective balance that gradient-based methods disrupt.

Evidence quality remains stable across datasets (Evi-F1 81.82 vs.\ 81.15 on DocRED), and the EDCR reduction ($-0.046$) mirrors the DocRED pattern, further supporting the robustness of CED-based selection.

The gap magnitude is stable across scales and architectures (range: 18.9--21.9pp), and model ranking is perfectly preserved (Spearman $\rho{=}1.0$), indicating that the absolute drop reflects the test annotation scheme rather than a model-specific deficiency. 266	\label{sec:error_analysis}
267	
268	Table~\ref{tab:error_analysis} decomposes the extraction improvements from RSFT into error categories across three scales. Three mechanisms drive the gains consistently:
269	
270	\paragraph{Truncation false negatives.} SFT models frequently hit the generation length limit, producing incomplete outputs that miss triples. RSFT training on compact, high-quality outputs reduces this truncation rate. The effect is strongest at 1.7B ($-841$ truncation FN, $-22$\%), where the SFT model's output length is least controlled.
271	
272	\paragraph{Hallucinated false positives.} CED-based filtering removes training examples with unfaithful predictions, reducing the rate of hallucinated triples at inference. LLaMA benefits most ($-593$ hallucinated FP, $-11.8$\%), suggesting cross-architecture variation in hallucination susceptibility.
273	
274	\paragraph{Duplicate predictions.} RSFT training data, selected for quality, contains fewer repetitive patterns. This propagates to inference, reducing duplicate triples by $11$--$20$\% across scales, with 1.7B showing the largest reduction ($-20.2$\%).
275	
276	\paragraph{Evidence quality unchanged.} Despite substantial extraction improvements, evidence exact-match F1 changes by less than 0.4pp at every scale. RSFT selects for joint extraction-evidence quality, but the evidence signal in CED scoring does not translate into measurable evidence improvement. This suggests that evidence grounding requires targeted optimization (e.g., evidence-specific rewards in RL) rather than data selection alone.
277	
278	\paragraph{Residual difficulty.} The proportion of ``other'' false negatives (triples missed for reasons beyond truncation or formatting) increases by 13--15\% in relative terms after RSFT. As easy errors (truncation, duplication) are eliminated, the remaining error distribution shifts toward harder cases: cross-sentence reasoning, implicit relations, and long-tail entity pairs. The relation types with the largest RSFT gains (participant, conflict, league, screenwriter, operator, contains\_administrative\_territory) involve cross-sentence reasoning or long-tail entities, consistent with RSFT's selection pressure toward diverse, high-quality outputs.

302	\label{sec:edcr_per_relation}
303	
304	Computing EDCR for each of the 76 relation types with $\geq$5 evaluation samples (from the RSFT CED s42 model) reveals that per-relation EDCR correlates strongly with per-relation Rel-F1 ($\rho = -0.79$, $n = 76$, $p < 0.001$), confirming its utility as a difficulty indicator. Filtering to types with $\geq$5 predictions strengthens the correlation ($\rho = -0.85$, $n = 74$, $p < 0.001$). Per-relation EDCR is statistically independent of Evi-F1 ($\rho = -0.06$, $p = 0.58$), and Evi-F1 itself shows no association with Rel-F1 ($\rho = -0.01$, $p = 0.91$). These null correlations establish that evidence quality and extraction ability are fully decoupled across relation types. Extreme cases illustrate the diagnostic power: \texttt{date\_of\_birth} has EDCR $= 0.118$ (highly faithful, with extraction and evidence tightly coupled), while \texttt{head\_of\_government} reaches $0.956$ (highly decoupled). This per-relation analysis avoids the shared-component concern present in cross-method EDCR-vs-Rel-F1 correlation, providing independent validation of EDCR's diagnostic utility.

314	\section{Qualitative Analysis}
315	\label{sec:qualitative}
316	
317	We present representative examples illustrating three phenomena: evidence quality differences between SFT and RSFT, GRPO format gaming under catastrophic collapse, and per-relation EDCR diagnostics.
318	
319	\paragraph{Case 1: Evidence quality.}
320	Table~\ref{tab:case_evidence} compares evidence citations from SFT and RSFT on three documents. SFT tends to cite many sentences indiscriminately, including distractors unrelated to the target triple, while RSFT selects precisely the gold evidence sentences. For \emph{America's Sweetheart}, SFT cites 6 sentences (precision 0.17) whereas RSFT cites only the single correct sentence (precision 1.00). The pattern is consistent: SFT achieves evidence precision of 0.00--0.20 across these examples, while RSFT achieves 1.00 in all three cases.
321

323	\centering

333	America's Sweetheart & (record label, country, United States) & 0.17 & 1.00 & 6 \\
334	Jade (Mortal Kombat) & (Jade, present in work, Mortal Kombat) & 0.20 & 1.00 & 5 \\
335	\bottomrule
336	\end{tabular}%
337	}
338	\end{table}
339	
340	\paragraph{Case 2: GRPO format gaming.}
341	Under catastrophic collapse (GRPO QLoRA $G{=}4$), the model abandons the DocRED 96-type relation ontology and generates free-text relation labels. On the document \emph{Something to Believe In}, the model produces 35 predicted triples with relations such as ``is a'', ``honor'', and ``location'', none of which belong to the target ontology. All 35 predictions are incorrect. Similarly, for \emph{J\'{o}zef Pi\l{}sudski Monument}, 28 predictions use non-standard relations with 0 correct matches. The model retains the structural format of triple-with-evidence output but fills it with fabricated relation types. The model produces well-formed evidence for these non-existent relations.
342	
343	\paragraph{Case 3: EDCR diagnostics.}
344	Per-relation EDCR identifies specific relation types where extraction and evidence are misaligned. For \texttt{date\_of\_birth} (EDCR $= 0.118$), the model's evidence consistently matches gold annotations: both extraction and evidence point to the same biographical sentence. In contrast, \texttt{notable\_work} (EDCR $= 0.941$) exhibits severe decoupling: the model cites sentence [0] (a general introduction) instead of the gold evidence sentence [3] (which contains the actual work attribution). High-EDCR relations tend to involve indirect or multi-hop reasoning where surface-level context misleads the evidence generator.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
\begin{abstract}

Large Language Model (LLM) based Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) now matches or exceeds encoder baselines in extraction accuracy, yet these methods output bare relation triplets without identifying which sentences support each prediction.
Deployment contexts such as clinical knowledge bases and legal due-diligence systems require verifiable evidence that users can trace to source text.
Encoder-based evidence methods (SAIS, DREEAM) provide supporting sentences but trail LLM approaches in accuracy, leaving a gap between extraction performance and output verifiability.

We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as a structured generation task and compare Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT) across three fully evaluated scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B validation, two model families, and two datasets.
The na\"{i}ve expectation is that evidence generation always costs extraction accuracy. Our experiments reveal that this cost is not fixed but forms a landscape shaped by capacity, paradigm, and data quality. Within the Qwen3 family (on the development set), evidence is beneficial at 1.7B ($-$5.63pp Ign-F1) but approximately neutral at $\geq$4B (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp at 4B; positive $=$ cost). Gradient-based optimization amplifies evidence-extraction competition (GRPO catastrophic, DPO gradual), while RSFT with Natural Language Inference (NLI) based scoring avoids decoupling entirely through output filtering rather than gradient pressure.

RSFT compresses training seed variance 7.5--31$\times$ on Qwen3 and 4.6$\times$ on LLaMA (complete pairwise seed separation, Cohen's $d{=}2.58$). Our 1.7B RSFT model (51.19 Ign-F1, std 0.09pp) approaches 8B Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) performance (50.19, std 3.23pp) at 4.7$\times$ fewer parameters. Test-set evaluation preserves model ranking across all evaluated scales (Spearman $\rho{=}1.0$).

\end{abstract}
